sections.title: Alchemy on the page and in the world
sections.intro: How alchemy reaches the page and the field: the bench, the alchemist's voice, Drafts in a fight, medicine, forensics, money and the made dead. The alchemy conversion's 131 answers (R61) set the doctrine; these ask only how it shows.

questions.title: Bench work on the page
questions.question: When a scene makes a Draft, how much of the bench procedure goes on the page, and in what form?
questions.context: R70-46 asks for 'tool, material and steps in order' in at least one stretch; R70-75 sets a rite as a numbered Guild form, performed, then departed from. Alchemetrica gives every operation its sequence (the Twelve Turnings: Reading, Burning, Rot, Wedding, Feeding and on). No row says whether bench work takes the rite's form.

options.label: One stretch, the floor
options.consequence: R70-46's floor only: one stretch of process per bench scene and the finished Draft looked at; the rest passes in a line. verify_scene changes nothing. Bench scenes stay short.
options.sample: Wenna Thorley set the flask in the cradle and laid the grounded rod against its shoulder. The rupture-quartz was packed to the neck, grey and fine as flour. She turned the crank. A thread of sound rose under the glass, then a hum in her back teeth, climbing. When it stopped climbing she stopped. The hum held. She struck the End seal into the wax with the brass die and chalked the hour on the cork. Good work had a look to it: the wax flat and unbubbled, the glass quiet against her palm.

options.label: Every step, in order
options.consequence: The whole sequence runs as prose whenever a Draft is made on the page, with no set-apart form. Bench scenes grow long, and a reader could repeat the charging from the text.
options.sample: Wenna Thorley dried the cradle with a rag and checked the rod's ground strap where it bolted to the floor plate. Then the flask, seated upright, and the rod laid against its shoulder where the glass thickened. The rupture-quartz inside was packed to the neck. She turned the crank slowly and evenly until the hum came, and kept turning while it climbed, and stopped the moment it held level. The rod came away clean. She struck the End seal into the wax with the brass die. The wax dulled. She chalked the hour on the cork.

options.label: Guild form, then performed
options.consequence: The scene's main brew appears first as the house's numbered form, set apart (R70-75 extended to the bench), then is performed, and something departs from it. Minor bench work keeps A's single stretch.
options.sample:
*Form of Charging. Thundercrack Grenade. Reserved to Expert hands.*
*I. The rod is set to ground. II. The crank is turned until the hum holds. III. The End seal is struck. IV. The hour is written on the cork.*
Wenna Thorley did the first three as the form had them, the hum climbing in her back teeth and levelling. At the fourth her chalk was gone from the tray. She wrote the hour on the cork in soot with a wet thumb, which the form did not allow, and which would smear in the first pocket it went into.

questions.rec_reason: You chose numbered rites and documents yesterday; the form plants a Draft's rules before the fight that spends it (R70-71), and the departure is where a bench scene finds its drama.

questions.title: Heat at the Draw Age bench
questions.question: What heats an alchemist's bench in a Guild city of the Draw Age?
questions.context: Alchemetrica's benches burn charcoal in the Long Furnace and hold the Rot in the dung Bed, which every attempted replacement has done worse than. R59-01 has draw-fed engines replace coal and steam outright; R53-02 leaves small fires to the poor edge. No row says whether a rich house heats its stills from the main. C-137 (thermometers) stays with the docket.

options.label: Old fire everywhere
options.consequence: Alchemetrica stands as written: charcoal, the Long Furnace and the Bed in every house, rich or poor. The main lights the room and nothing else. A Guild-city workshop smells of charcoal like a village one.
options.sample: The Draft-house stood on Assay Row in Urbis, where every shopfront hummed, and its back room smelled of charcoal anyway. Tobin Garr knelt at the Long Furnace and listened for the settle as the fuel dropped down the tower. The sand bath above it had to stay below a simmer. He held his palm over it, drew the hand back sooner than he liked, and nodded. Above him the Essence lamps burned without a flicker over a bench where nothing else ran on the main.

options.label: Draw heat, the Bed kept
options.consequence: Guild-city houses run baths, stills and furnaces off trade supply, priced on the bill (R53-17); the Bed stays for the Rot, as canon defends it; charcoal holds in the provinces and the north.
options.sample: The Draft-house on Assay Row in Urbis ran its stills off the trade main, and the meter by the door ticked over whenever Tobin Garr opened a valve. He turned the sand bath's array down a mark and listened to the hum beneath it drop a note. Behind him, against the outer wall, the Bed steamed in its brick crib, the vessels buried to the shoulder in fermenting dung. The house had tried a draw-warmed cabinet for the Rot once. The ledger still carried the loss.

options.label: Fuel by purse
options.consequence: Fuel follows money inside every city: houses on trade supply heat from the main, poor houses burn charcoal and dung, and a bench's heat names its owner's class on sight. The Bed stays everywhere.
options.sample: Two streets apart in Urbis, the same operation ran on two fires. At the chartered house on Assay Row, Tobin Garr eased a valve and the sand bath warmed off the trade main, the meter ticking by the door. In the lane behind the tannery, Widow Pell fed charcoal to a clay furnace with a bent spoon and wiped the soot off her lids. Both houses kept a Bed against the back wall, steaming. Pell's batch would sell for less. Her customers knew the smell of it.

questions.rec_reason: It honours R59-01 (the main replaced coal) and keeps the Bed canon already defends, while R59-05's gradient leaves the provinces and the north on charcoal, so a Kharven bench still smells of the old fire.

questions.title: The alchemist's voice
questions.question: Which habits make an alchemist's speech and noticing unswappable on the page?
questions.context: R48-41 has characters talk magic 'by their training'; R61-91 writes Draftcraft 'in price, vessel, seal and ledger'. The Fleshshapers (R24-1) show a trade idiom: anatomy 'applied to everything'. Alchemetrica adds the trade's own bodies (Draft-mark, crucible palsy) and a room where talk at the wrong moment of a Feeding costs a master a month. Tick every habit that should stand.

options.label: Reads the body first
options.consequence: Every alchemist notices mouths, hands, sclera and tremor before faces, and reads a dose, a career or a lie in them. Each alchemist's card gains a 'reads first' line in its voice block.
options.sample: The sergeant asked whether the Bone-Grey would keep past six hours. Ilse Varrow answered his mouth first, in her head. His gums were swollen. He swallowed more often than a man with nothing on his mind ought to: the spit of somebody being dosed with calomel past what his gut needed. A regimental surgeon who liked his quicksilver. 'Six hours, then it takes what the wound needed,' she said. 'And tell your surgeon to stop purging you.'

options.label: Price, vessel, seal, ledger
options.consequence: Every alchemist weighs a thing by what it cost, what holds it, whose mark closes it and where it is entered; their speech prices before it praises. Extends R61-91 from the texts to every alchemist on the page.
options.sample: The sergeant asked whether the Bone-Grey would keep past six hours. Ilse Varrow turned the packet over first and found the Legion's stamp on the wax, a quartermaster's lot at six-tenths of a silver mark. 'Whose lot is this, and when was it entered?' she said. 'Six hours on the wound, Sergeant. After that it takes what the wound needed, and the ledger won't care which.'

options.label: Bench words for everything
options.consequence: The operations become all-purpose idiom: a plan still in the Rot, a recruit fed too fast, a match made with no glyphs down. The Fleshshaper model (R24-1) applied to the trade, logged a few per card.
options.sample: The sergeant asked whether the Bone-Grey would keep past six hours. 'It keeps,' Ilse Varrow said. 'It just stops being on your side. Four hours it draws, and after that it's a Feeding gone too fast, and a thing fed too fast finishes the nearest version of itself.' She pushed the packet across. 'Your wound's still in the Rot. Leave it black. Don't open it to look.'

options.label: Quiet at the work
options.consequence: Talk is rationed near a working: an alchemist answers in the fewest words and counts under the breath at the Feeding. Silence becomes the trade's tell in any room.
options.sample: The sergeant asked whether the Bone-Grey would keep past six hours. Ilse Varrow held up a finger without turning from the Returner, her lips moving on a count. He waited. The count went on. Behind her the Long Furnace ticked as the charcoal settled. When the count was done she sealed the feed port and looked round at him over her spectacles. 'Six,' she said, and went back to the glass.

questions.rec_reason: Reading bodies gives the Kakashi-style read Isaac likes, price and ledger keep money before magic, and bench idiom makes alchemists unswappable; quiet at the work already follows from Alchemetrica and needs no new rule.

questions.title: Prepared or live in a fight
questions.question: When an alchemist fights, how much of the alchemy may be made during the fight itself?
questions.context: R70-71 plants a working's rules before the fight; R61-100 keeps Drafts reserve-free. The archive's one full alchemical fight (the Geturo arena run) made its vials weeks before, and Volume III makes chalk over dressed stone Draft ground if the hand means it. Nothing rules whether bench work may happen mid-exchange.

options.label: Made before, spent during
options.consequence: Every Draft in a fight left a bench before it began; the fight only spends the bandolier, and an earlier bench scene plants each vial (R70-71). The empty loop is the alchemist's clock.
options.sample: Ansel Dray had filled the bandolier in Urbis by lamplight, days before, against a man he had only read about. Half the loops were empty now. The practitioner across the yard had answered the first throws with heat, so Dray had spent the Null-Salt on the array at his feet, and the air between them had gone still and ordinary. He touched the next loop. Ashfang, for the blade. After that there was the knife, and whatever he could think of to say.

options.label: Plus Draft ground, live
options.consequence: As A, and a Draft-circle may be drawn mid-fight, as Volume III allows: the drawing costs whole turns with hands busy and eyes down, an opening the opponent can take.
options.sample: Half the loops were empty. Dray went to his knees on the flagstones with the chalk, because the yard was dressed stone and the manual said dressed stone would serve if the hand meant it. The circle had to close before it was ground at all. He drew with his head down and his back to the man he was fighting, which every instructor in the Division had told him never to do, and the boots on the stone came on behind him, and he kept drawing.

options.label: Live bench in the field
options.consequence: Stocks may be mixed, charged or fed in the field mid-fight, priced in turns and in the formula's own failure risk. The alchemist fights as a workshop on legs, and fights run longer.
options.sample: Half the loops were empty. Dray thumbed the stopper off a vial of base stock and tipped the last of the seed liquor into it, swirling, his eyes on the man across the yard instead of on the glass. The mix clouded, then cleared. A Feeding done in a hurry finished the nearest version of itself, and he had done this one in a hurry. He threw it anyway, because there was no time left to find out which version he had made.

questions.rec_reason: Preparation wins fights here as it does in Mother of Learning, and the planted bench scene keeps the read fair; live Draft ground is already canon and costs turns, a window the opponent can punish.

questions.title: A Draft in the six-second turn
questions.question: How long does using a Draft take inside a fight's six-second turn, and what does it open?
questions.context: R47-11 makes a combat turn six seconds. Canon gives no use time for any Draft; Aperture Wound Ichor must go on inside the first minute, and Active Recovery needs the fighter to stop. Inside roughly twenty feet the fencing grammar takes over (R11-5) and a fired gun becomes a club. This sets the alchemist's version of the reload.

options.label: A drink costs the turn
options.consequence: Drinking or smearing takes a whole turn and is an opening inside measure; throwing or smashing is one action within an exchange. The hand going to the bandolier becomes a readable tell.
options.sample: Maera Cole backed out of measure, or tried to. The Shirogane blade followed her, patient. She thumbed the cork off the Equilibrium Draught with her off hand, and it took the whole of a turn to get the glass to her mouth, swallow, and get the hand back to the hilt. He used every part of that turn. The cut came in under her raised elbow. She took it along the ribs, with the Draught already damping the panic that should have answered it.

options.label: Never inside measure
options.consequence: No Draft is drunk or applied inside measure at all; use happens before contact or after a break of measure, and a scene that breaks this fails the floor (R13-4).
options.sample: Maera Cole wanted the Equilibrium Draught and could not have it. The Shirogane blade was a pace off, inside the distance where a hand leaving the hilt was a hand lost. She gave ground instead, step after step, until the pillar stood between them and the bind was broken. Only then did her off hand find the bandolier. She drank with her eyes on the pillar's edge, and her fear went flat and far away.

options.label: Fast as the hand
options.consequence: Use takes the moment a hand takes, folded into the exchange with no stated turn cost; the price lies only in the Draft's own effect and failure.
options.sample: Maera Cole thumbed the cork off the Equilibrium Draught between his second cut and his third and had it down in a swallow, the glass gone over her shoulder before it could break. The Shirogane blade came on. Her fear had gone flat and far away. The next parry came easy, almost lazy, and later the surgeon would ask her why she had not felt the cut along her ribs until the fight was over.

questions.rec_reason: Real hands need seconds to uncork and swallow, so the reload logic carries over; the reach for the vial becomes a tell the opponent can read, which keeps Drafts fair and counterable.

questions.title: Who carries it onto a field
questions.question: Who carries combat Drafts onto a field, and how common are they?
questions.context: The Standing Index gates every lot by a named rank (Apprentice up to Paragon), and the Alchemical Index files the Thundercrack Grenade as Expert work. Canon already issues Bone-Grey Compress to the Legion and burns Will-Break at the line; R46-4 says a practitioner 'cannot equip an army'. Nothing sets how often a field sees alchemy.

options.label: Specialists only
options.consequence: Combat Drafts belong to alchemists and sappers with bandoliers; the line carries Bone-Grey and nothing more. A thrown charge on a field is an event, and a reader can count the alchemists.
options.sample: The line stood easy in the frost while the quartermaster's cart went down it. Every man got a Bone-Grey packet and nothing else, slipped into the pouch behind the cartridge box. The sappers had their own cart. A handful of men in stained coats, bandoliers crossed on their chests, stood apart the way men stand apart from a thing that might go off. The line watched them the way it watched the sky.

options.label: Issue by gate
options.consequence: Drafts reach a field by their rank gate: low-gate lots to the line, Adept munitions to drilled details, Expert charges only to Expert hands. The gate becomes the field's ration logic.
options.sample: The quartermaster's cart went down the line in the frost. Every man got a Bone-Grey packet, and the corporals got Ward-Chalk as well, for the camp tonight. Behind the line a detail knelt by an iron brazier with Will-Break cakes stacked beside it, waiting on the wind. The Thundercrack flasks never came down the line at all. They hung humming on the bandolier of the one woman in the company certified to carry them.

options.label: Gates, bought by purse
options.consequence: As B, and a company's purse decides how many certified hands it retains, priced on the approved retainer table, so rich companies field far more alchemy than poor ones.
options.sample: The Guard company's cart went down the line with more on it than the levy's ever had. Bone-Grey for every man, and behind the line a row of certified hands on retainer, Adept and Expert, their bandoliers humming. Each of them cost the company more a month than a whole section of the men in front of them. Across the frost the levy had a single sapper, and he was drunk.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps canon's gates as the ration and adds money before magic: a rich company fields more certified hands at retainer-table prices, so the alchemy on a field tells a reader who paid for the war.

questions.title: The formula's own failure
questions.question: Every combat formula in the Index fails onto its own user through its own mechanism; how does that risk show on the page?
questions.context: The Alchemical Index's design rule: Ashfang lights on the wielder's own nick first, a Thundercrack carried more than an hour past charging goes off by itself, Obsidian Fang numbs the poisoner's bare fingers. R47-9 lets opponents induce a working's failures; R47-3 makes counters facts players can work out.

options.label: Handling as a tell
options.consequence: Every use shows the precaution its formula demands (the gloved hand, the chalked hour, the edge kept off the wielder's skin), and a reading opponent may exploit it. The counter is always on the page.
options.sample: The Accord duellist fought with his off hand gloved to the wrist and never let it near his own blade. Haro Venn had watched him across two passes and seen it both times: the elbow tucked, the edge carried wide of his body like a lamp through a draughty room. A coated edge, then, and one that cared whose blood it found. Venn stopped trying for the sword arm. He went for the gloved hand instead.

options.label: The risk fires
options.consequence: As A, and each formula carried through an arc fails onto its user at least once on the page, so the failure modes stay real. Some bandoliers kill their owners.
options.sample: The Accord duellist fought with his off hand gloved and his edge carried wide of his body, and for a while it held. Then Haro Venn's parry drove the flat back along the man's own forearm, and the coating found the scratch it opened. The wax took the blood and lit. The duellist screamed and dropped the blade, and the smell of his arm cooking spread across the yard.

options.label: In the notes
options.consequence: Failure modes stay in the author notes and the formula's entry unless the scene turns on them; the page shows the Draft working. Fights run cleaner and faster.
options.sample: The Accord duellist's blade came in fast, and where it touched Haro Venn's forearm the cut sealed itself black and smoking, and the pain under the seal kept burning after the blade had gone. Venn gave ground. The coating was good work. He would read about it later in the surgeon's ledger, and learn there what it cost the man who carried it.

questions.rec_reason: Isaac wants fair abilities with findable counters: the handling is the tell, an opponent can read it in two or three exchanges, and the formula's real cost stays visible without killing every alchemist who carries it.

questions.title: Poison and the duel
questions.question: Is a poisoned or coated edge lawful and honourable in a duel, and who decides?
questions.context: R70-101 gives a duel a full declaration with a price; R70-105 keys rites to culture; R53-11 borrows each culture's real justice, and R70-45 makes law an Inventory field. The Apparatus page says the Accord classes offensive Drafts as munitions. No row says whether a coated edge must be declared, or what it costs a fighter's name.

options.label: Declared, or it's murder
options.consequence: A coated edge must be named in the declaration (R70-101); used undeclared, the killing is murder in every culture. One law everywhere, and the declaration gains a line.
options.sample: Haro Venn gave his name, his house and his teacher's name, as the hall required. Then he laid the blade flat across both palms so the second could see the dull sheen along the edge. 'Slag-Iron,' he said. 'A cut from this seals as it lies. Your surgeon will have to open it again.' The hall went quiet. His opponent nodded once. The steward wrote it into the book beside the date, in a careful clerk's hand that took its time.

options.label: By culture, on the Inventory
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory gains a line on coated weapons and poison, taken from the culture's real analogue; the Accord's munitions class is the first entry. An Accord duel and a Moto duel may differ.
options.sample: Haro Venn gave his name and his house. The Accord steward did not ask about the sheen on the edge; he asked for the stamp. Under hall rules a coated blade counted as munitions, lawful with a Bench entry and nothing else asked. Venn produced the slip. The steward checked the mark against his register and wrote 'Slag-Iron, entered' beside the date. Nobody in the gallery thought the less of him. Other halls kept other laws.

options.label: Lawful everywhere
options.consequence: A coating is equipment like the edge itself; no culture stigmatises it, and only the dead man's kin and the ordinary law of killing apply. Alchemy becomes plain duelling kit.
options.sample: Haro Venn gave his name and his house and drew. The sheen along his edge drew no comment from the steward or the gallery; many of the blades in that hall carried something. His opponent glanced at it once, the way a man glances at another man's guard, and took his measure a hand's width longer than he had meant to.

questions.rec_reason: Law is already an Inventory field (R70-45) and the Accord's munitions class is canon; a culture-keyed answer gives duels the texture rites have under R70-105, and an undeclared coating can still be murder wherever a culture says so.

questions.title: A Draft's readout
questions.question: What readout does a Draft carry, and does it earn a line when it is used?
questions.context: R70-95 gives an item one card at purchase or appraisal: Tier, Latin form, Grade band, maker, stamp, price, lore. The Standing Index marks every lot by Provenance Class, Fidelity and Carry. R70-85 earns in-scene readouts only at an appraisal, a wound and Essence spent, and R70-86 caps them at three a scene. No row fits a Draft.

options.label: Card once, body at use
options.consequence: R70-95's card gains the Index's three marks and prints the gate by name; it appears once, at purchase or appraisal. At use only the body shows, plus a surgeon's wound line if a wound earns one.
options.sample:
Sergeant Holm paid the sutler and turned the brown bottle to the lamp.
[CUTWATER TINCTURE · Household · Class III · Fidelity C · Carry 8 · Brannock's lot · 0.15 silver mark · Spoils. The label does not say when.]
In the ditch he poured it into the cut along his forearm. It foamed white and stung like a slap, and the small vessels at the edges stopped weeping. The cut itself stayed open, as wide as before.

options.label: Card plus a dose line
options.consequence: As A, plus one line at use (what went in, the onset, what it will do), printed as a surgeon's or instrument's line and counted in R70-86's three. This reopens R70-85 by adding a fourth moment.
options.sample:
Sergeant Holm paid the sutler for the brown bottle.
[CUTWATER TINCTURE · Household · Class III · Fidelity C · Carry 8 · 0.15 silver mark]
In the ditch he poured it into the cut along his forearm. It foamed white and stung like a slap.
[Applied: Cutwater, open wound, forearm. Small vessels closing. Tissue not knit.]
The weeping at the edges stopped. The cut itself stayed as wide as before.

options.label: Assay tape, no card
options.consequence: No card at purchase: when a lot is assayed, the Bench's coil prints a tape in its own type (R70-77) carrying the three marks. Ordinary buyers see only a label, and nothing prints at use.
options.sample:
The sutler owned no coil, so Sergeant Holm bought the brown bottle on its label and the sutler's word. It was the depot quartermaster who ran the lot through the assay coil, after some of the men's cuts had gone bad, and the tape came out of the slot in the Bench's narrow type:
[CUTWATER · III · C · 8 · LOT SPOILED]
The quartermaster tore it off and went to find the sutler.

questions.rec_reason: It uses the card Isaac already chose with the Index's own marks; at use, R70-85's wound line already covers what a Draft does to a body, so no new readout moment is needed and the cap stays honest.

questions.title: Medicine by place and purse
questions.question: Which medicine treats a wound on the page: period practice, alchemical Drafts, or both sorted by place and purse?
questions.context: R53-10 gives Guild cities 'what their decade has (anaesthesia, antisepsis...)' and the north and the poor 'folk medicine and the barber'. Canon issues Bone-Grey Compress to the Legion, and the price table puts a surgeon at 5 to 40 gold. R60-02 keeps real healing times. Nothing sets where Drafts sit beside carbolic and chloroform.

options.label: Drafts first
options.consequence: In Guild cities the physician-alchemist's Drafts are the medicine and period practice is the poor's; a wound scene names its Drafts and their clocks. Alchemy displaces the period surgeon.
options.sample: The physician-alchemist cut the trouser leg away and packed the wound with Bone-Grey before she said a word. He screamed once. 'Four hours,' she told the orderly. 'Then it comes out, whatever it looks like. Past six it starts taking what the wound needs.' She chalked the hour on the man's boot. Nobody on that ward had seen a bone saw in years. The saws hung in the barber's window down the street, for people who could not pay for grey paste.

options.label: Period first, Drafts dear
options.consequence: The surgeon's carbolic, chloroform and silk are the norm in Guild cities; Drafts are costly extras, rationed and argued over. Medicine reads Victorian, and alchemy is a luxury.
options.sample: The surgeon washed the wound with carbolic until the man screamed, then had the orderly hold the chloroform cloth to his face until he stopped. Silk, a curved needle, the edges drawn together in a neat ladder of knots. The Bone-Grey stayed in its locked case. The ward had a handful of packets left for the month, and the surgeon would not spend one on a clean thigh wound in a man who could afford to lie still.

options.label: By place and purse
options.consequence: Both, sorted by money and map: the Legion gets Bone-Grey by issue, a Guild city's purse buys the surgeon and his Drafts, the north and the poor get the barber and Cutwater. Every wound scene names which.
options.sample: In the Legion's tent the orderly packed the thigh wound with Bone-Grey and chalked the hour on the man's boot, because the Legion paid for grey paste and nothing better. In Urbis the same wound would have bought chloroform, carbolic, silk and a surgeon's fee in gold. On the road north it would have bought a barber, a bottle of Cutwater of uncertain age, and whatever the barber happened to know.

questions.rec_reason: It is R53-10 and the price table made exact, money before magic in the infirmary; the same wound costing three different things in three places is grimdark texture with real history under it.

questions.title: Proving a poison
questions.question: Can a poisoning be proved in the Draw Age, and by what test?
questions.context: Canon has no poison test and no antidote. The coil reads Essence residue, so a worked poison leaves a signature and plain white arsenic leaves none. Real chemistry inside the span has the arsenic mirror test (1836), the copper-foil test (1841) and freshly made iron rust as an arsenic antidote (1834). R53-15 lets folk beliefs stand uncorrected.

options.label: Real tests, by place
options.consequence: The Real Alchemy gains the mirror test, the copper test and the iron antidote under in-world names, present where R59-05's gradient puts them: Guild cities have them, the north does not. The coil reads worked poisons.
options.sample: The Watch chemist ran the stomach washings into the flask with zinc and acid and lit the gas at the jet. He held a cold porcelain dish in the flame. A dark spot bloomed on the white, silver-black and shining. It spread. 'There's your arsenic,' he said, and slid the dish across for the walker to sign. She signed it. Upstairs, the cook who had tasted the soup was drinking a brown slurry of fresh iron rust the physician had mixed for her.

options.label: Coil only
options.consequence: No plain poison test exists; only worked poisons leave a signature the coil reads. White arsenic becomes the perfect murder, and the Watch knows it: a gap a poisoner can plan around.
options.sample: The walker ran the coil over the dead merchant from crown to heel. The needle never stirred. Whatever had killed him had carried no working, so she wrote 'no residue' in the field book and underlined it, because that was all the book could hold. Downstairs the widow signed for the body. Everyone in the house knew about the white powder in the kitchen. Nobody could prove it was anything but rat poison, bought for rats.

options.label: Folk tests that lie
options.consequence: No real test exists; folk tests stand in and are half right: a silver spoon blackens in crude arsenic (sulphur in the old ore) and stays bright in refined white arsenic. Juries convict on them. R53-15 leaves them uncorrected.
options.sample: The walker stirred the dead merchant's soup with the silver spoon and held it to the lamp. Bright as the day it was polished. 'Clean,' she said, and wrote it down, and the widow let out her breath. In the kitchen cupboard behind them, beside the salt, sat a paper of white powder with an Accord refinery's stamp on the fold, bought, the cook said later, for the rats.

questions.rec_reason: Real physics with findable counters: a careful reader can catch a poisoner, the north's lack of the test is the gradient doing grimdark work, and the silver spoon can live on in the north as an uncorrected folk belief.

questions.title: A forensic reading on the page
questions.question: How does a residue reading, the Night Watch's forensic work, go on the page?
questions.context: The Necrocursica's protocol: never alone, one reader inside the radius and one outside, the gauge read aloud at every stand, and 'the contradiction is the diagnosis'. R61-112 has the investigator log readings at scenes; R48-16 lets anyone with an instrument state figures. R70-86 caps readouts at three a scene, but figures in a mouth sit outside that cap.

options.label: Protocol as action
options.consequence: The pair, the stands and the withdrawal play as action, and figures enter in a mouth, read aloud at every stand, outside R70-86's cap. The contradiction between the readers is the scene's turn.
options.sample: Farrant stood at the gate at the foot of the stair and read the gauge up to Dessa Mael, three flights above her. 'Tenth division. Twenty-one.' The needle crept. 'Twenty-one, climbing.' She carried the coil to the next stand and read again, and again coil and gauge would not agree, the same way at every stand. Her left hand had warmed. A taste came up at the back of her throat, metal and something sweet. Then Dessa was calling her title down the stair, twice.

options.label: Field-book lines set in
options.consequence: The investigator's log entries are set into the scene in her book's house style (R12-4's document voice) and the prose runs between them. The figures stay on paper; the body stays in the prose.
options.sample:
*Gauge, the gate at the foot of the stair, tenth division: twenty-one, climbing while I held it.*
Farrant wrote it with the pencil's stub against the wall, then carried the coil a stand along and wrote again.
*Coil and gauge disagree. The same way at every stand.*
Her left hand had warmed. She did not write that down. A taste came up at the back of her throat, metal and something sweet, and the next line in the book was in another hand, Dessa Mael's, from three flights up. *Fifty breaths. Counted.*

options.label: Finding only
options.consequence: The reading passes in a line and the finding is the beat; procedure and figures go to the author notes. Forensic scenes run short and land on what was found.
options.sample: Farrant read the stair gate with coil and gauge, stand by stand, and they disagreed the same way every time: something below the town was being taken, and in quantity. She did not remember stopping. Dessa Mael's voice came down the stair, calling her title, and Farrant found herself sitting on the bottom step with a taste of metal and sugar in her mouth and the gauge still in her hand.

questions.rec_reason: Figures read aloud are LitRPG crunch that costs nothing against the readout cap, the pair protocol is canon procedure with tension built in, and a Class Ø reader voicing numbers she cannot feel makes a strong, findable read.

questions.title: Corruption shown on the body
questions.question: When an alchemist's Great Work turns corrupt, which signs reach the page?
questions.context: The Heresiology lists bodily signs (metallic sweat, ash under the nails that matches no reagent, nosebleeds when a concealment succeeds, a cold patch over the heart) and signs in the work (vessels that crack under one operator, sigils that correct themselves darker). R61-85 gives every corruption a named, findable counter; R48-30 wants surprises foreshadowed. Tick every kind that should show.

options.label: Signs in the body
options.consequence: The Heresiology's bodily signs become standing tells, planted before any reveal and one a scene at most, so a reader can catch a corrupt master before the plot names him.
options.sample: Pim had luted joints for Master Corvane for years and knew his hands better than his face. Lately they sweated at the bench, a fine grey sweat that smelled of a coin held too long in a fist. There was ash under his nails that matched nothing in the rack. Pim checked the rack twice. He told himself the master had been at the calcination bench, and luted the next joint, and did not ask.

options.label: Signs in the work
options.consequence: The bench betrays him first: vessels crack under his hands alone, inscriptions darken on their own, residue gathers in shapes. The workshop shows the corruption before the man does.
options.sample: Pim had luted joints for Master Corvane for years and had never seen a vessel lost at the Wedding. This month the Returners had cracked on the master's bench and nowhere else in the house. The glyph ring round the newest one had been chalked pale that morning. By evening it had darkened, line by line, to the colour of an old bruise, and nobody had touched it.

options.label: Signs in technique
options.consequence: A corrupted practitioner's workings run their corrupted versions (the Open Crucible's model, where Honest Fire strips structure it finds inconvenient), so the tell lives in how he works and fights.
options.sample: Master Corvane put his hand on the cracked lintel to steady the stair, and the working he had always used for that held the stone where it lay. This time it did more. Pim watched the carved leaves on the lintel smooth away under the master's palm, the ornament gone back to plain dressed stone, as though Corvane had judged the carving unnecessary. The stair held. Corvane went on up without looking at what he had done.

options.label: Only when the vow breaks
options.consequence: Corruption is written only at its event, a Shear Break when the vow fails, with the fall shown whole and no slow signs before it.
options.sample: Master Corvane had sworn on his circle's seal never to render from the living. The night he did it, Pim was luting by the wall. The master set the stock in the vessel and something in him gave, audibly, a crack like a joint going in cold weather. He sat down on the floor of his own workshop with his hands open and could not remember the formula he had written himself.

questions.rec_reason: Slow, findable tells in body, bench and technique are the Bleach-style late reveal done fairly: every sign planted before it is named, so the fall lands as recognition, and the Shear Break stays available as the event at the end.

questions.title: Accidents and fumes
questions.question: When bench work fails (a lute vents, a Wedding ruptures), how is the accident written?
questions.context: Alchemetrica: a failed lute vents Strongwater fume, which kills everyone in a closed workshop in the order they stood nearest. Strongwater is nitric acid; its red-orange fume is nitrogen dioxide, which in real chemistry often kills hours later as the lungs fill. R12-6 gives every rite its list of errors; R49-46 frees science words for trained POVs.

options.label: Real time, real chemistry
options.consequence: The failure plays in the room as it happens (the crack, the colour, the cough, who stood nearest), and the dying runs on the real clock, some of it hours later. The physics carries the horror.
options.sample: The lute round the receiver's neck cracked with a sound like a dry twig, and red-orange fume came out of the crack in a thin ribbon and spread. Hask, at the receiver, breathed it first. He coughed once and went on coughing and made for the door with his sleeve over his mouth, and the rest went after him. Out in the yard they laughed about it, eyes streaming. By midnight Hask was drowning in his cot with no water anywhere near him.

options.label: Found after
options.consequence: The accident is met in its aftermath: the room found, the order of the dead read from where they lie, the cause worked out from the lute. The reader assembles the minute nobody saw.
options.sample: The walker opened the workshop door with a wet cloth over her face and waited for the air. Then she went in. The receiver stood on its bench with a crack in the lute round its neck and a rust-coloured bloom on the plaster above it. Hask lay nearest the still. The second Hand lay between the bench and the door. The boy who carried ash had nearly reached the latch. She wrote down the order in which they lay, because it was the order in which they had died.

options.label: In the record
options.consequence: The accident appears as an in-world incident entry in the Guild's flat house style, set apart (R51-33), and the scene plays only what follows. The document carries the deaths.
options.sample:
*Incident, Tanner's Yard distillery. Lute failure at the receiver of a Strongwater still, closed room. Present: the master, two Hands, the Luteboy. Dead within the hour: the Hand at the receiver. Dead by morning: the master and the second Hand. The house is fined for unventilated work. The Luteboy is not named, being among the dead.*
Bel Askew read the notice where it was pinned on the Guild board, went home, and opened every window in her room, though it was winter.

questions.rec_reason: Real chemistry makes the canon line exact and worse: the nearest die first, and the ones who walked out laughing die by morning. That is grimdark cost with real physics under it, which is Isaac's taste.

questions.title: The trade's paper in a scene
questions.question: Which parts of the trade's money and paper show whenever alchemy changes hands or gets used?
questions.context: R70-48 names every sum from the approved table and lets notable objects carry lineage; R11-3 makes proof-marks standing texture; Draycott's registered mark (R65-3) is struck on everything he makes; R61-111 puts an unentered sale's breach on the seller. The Standing Index prices lots in silver marks. Tick what should stand.

options.label: Price counted at use
options.consequence: Beyond R70-48's price at purchase, a fighter or worker counts what a Draft cost when he spends it, in his own money, the sum taken from the table or the Index. Money before magic, in the hand.
options.sample: Jory Fenn paid for two Deadlight Phials at the counter, a silver mark and a tenth apiece, and counted the coins out twice. Days down the shaft the first one gave out without warning, the way they did, and went to glittering dust in his palm. He cracked the second alight and thought, sourly, that he was walking into the dark holding more than a labourer's day of wages, and that it had better last.

options.label: The mark checked
options.consequence: Every lawful vessel carries its maker's registered mark, and anyone handling one looks at it the way a soldier reads a proof-dent (R11-3). The mark becomes standing texture and a trail.
options.sample: Jory Fenn turned each Deadlight Phial over before he paid. The wax on the stopper carried the house's mark, a lamp inside a ring, struck clean and deep. A shallow strike meant a tired hand or a copied die, and a copied die meant a phial that might die halfway down a shaft. He paid a silver mark and a tenth apiece. The clerk watched him check, and approved of it.

options.label: Provenance as plot
options.consequence: Lots can be forged, adulterated, stale or unentered, and a scene may turn on a bad lot; the forgery is always findable by mark, assay or the Index's own failure. A fair counter and a plot engine.
options.sample: The phial gave out in Jory Fenn's hand a day into the shaft, when it should have burned for two hundred hours. He stood in the black with its dust on his glove and did the arithmetic. The mark on the wax had been a lamp in a ring, struck shallow. He had noticed and paid anyway, because the counter on the corner was cheaper. Somewhere above him, a forger was eating well.

questions.rec_reason: All three are money before magic made concrete: the cost felt at use, the mark read like a proof-dent, and the bad lot as a fair, findable twist that a careful buyer could have caught.

questions.title: A Draft against a working
questions.question: When a Draft meets a ranked practitioner, what decides whether it touches him?
questions.context: R45-3 caps an enhancement at 'the Grade of whoever put the Essence into it'; R61-102 caps a pure alchemist's work at his bench Tier; R55-7 makes harmonic workings miss anyone at the caster's Stage or higher. Part Eleven's body Durability (Shell, Fortitude) answers plain force. Nothing says which of these a thrown Draft answers to.

options.label: Two parts, two answers
options.consequence: A Draft splits: its plain physics (blast, heat, acid, smoke) meets the target's body and Shell like any force, while its worked part answers the maker's Tier and fails against higher standing. Both traceable (R13-8).
options.sample: The Thundercrack burst on the flagstones at the Tenrai man's feet. The arc leapt for him and slid off, finding nothing it was allowed to take from a man so far above the woman who had charged it. The air took no notice of rank. The arc channel slammed outward in a thunderclap, and it struck him the way it struck the doorframe behind him, and he staggered with blood starting at one ear and his Shell humming from the blow.

options.label: Capped at maker's Tier
options.consequence: The whole Draft is a working at its maker's standing; a target above that standing takes nothing from it, blast included, as R55-7 does for harmonic workings. Alchemy never troubles the ranked.
options.sample: The Thundercrack burst on the flagstones at the Tenrai man's feet, and everything in it had come from the hands of a woman far below him. The arc and the thunderclap broke over him together, and he stood in them with his coat stirring, untouched, while behind him the doorframe split and the clerk who had been hiding there fell down holding both ears.

options.label: Plain force, no cap
options.consequence: A Draft is chemistry and charge: it lands in full on anyone in range, rank aside, and only the body's Durability answers it. Alchemy becomes the great leveller, and the ranked fear vials.
options.sample: The Thundercrack burst on the flagstones at the Tenrai man's feet, and the arc went into him through the soles of his boots, up the long bones of his legs and out at his knees. The thunderclap followed it. He went down on the stones with his legs jerking and blood at both ears, a man who had never in his life been hurt by anything a clerk could sell.

questions.rec_reason: It follows real physics (a blast is a blast) and existing law (worked effects cap at the maker), so a vial stays a real threat to the ranked through its physics while its working never outranks its maker; both counters are findable.

questions.title: A revenant in a fight
questions.question: When a revenant (a stalled Crossing) is met in a fight, what stops it?
questions.context: R61-77: a revenant is a body that spends its nine days where the Wellspring cannot take the residue, with habits, a direction and nothing that weighs them; it fades when diffusion completes, and moving it or Stillgate Ash is the counter. Canon is silent on wounds. The combat floor (R13-4) asks for injury by structure, and a corpse does not bleed.

options.label: Levers still rule
options.consequence: A body on habit: anatomy stops the motion (a cut hamstring drops it) while the habit keeps trying; only ash, removal or the ninth day ends it. The floor applies by structure, with no ATLS class.
options.sample: The dead pikeman got up late in his nine days and walked toward the line he had held, his left foot dragging where the ground had frozen it overnight. Corporal Ness let him come and swung the billhook low behind his knee. The hamstring parted like a wet rope and the leg folded. The pikeman went down on his face and kept on walking, his hands dragging him forward through the frost toward a line that was not there any more.

options.label: Only the counter ends it
options.consequence: Wounds do nothing, since the body has no need of its levers; only Stillgate Ash, moving it off the ground or diffusion ends a revenant. Fights against one are containment, never exchanges.
options.sample: The dead pikeman got up late in his nine days and walked toward the line he had held. Corporal Ness swung the billhook into the back of his knee and the hamstring parted, and the pikeman walked on the leg as though it were whole. Ness backed off. 'Ash,' he said. 'Get the ash.' Men from the detail ran for the cart while the dead man went on walking, toward a line that was not there any more.

options.label: Never a fight
options.consequence: Revenants are containment and aftermath work only, met by burial details with ash and carts; no exchange with one is ever written. They stay horror and logistics.
options.sample: The burial detail found the dead pikeman far from where they had left him, face down in the frost, still facing the line he had held. Ness ringed him with Stillgate Ash from the cart and stood back while the body went quiet, and then for a while after that, because the ash took from the living too. His fingers had gone numb to the wrist. They loaded the pikeman and moved on to the next.

questions.rec_reason: Real biomechanics keeps the fight readable and fair: the floor's injury by structure still works, the habit gives the read, and the canon counters still finish it, so a revenant becomes a Naruto-style puzzle with a clinical edge.

questions.title: The impression-body's voice
questions.question: How does the page render an impression-body, the likeness of the dead an alchemist pours and seals?
questions.context: R61-75 makes it a Greater Summons with the maker's own Core as its identity (Mu-jin's gloss: 'he summons himself'), reaching the dead's Volitional Trace; it ends at once when the held decision is delivered. R61-110 lets a trained reader find a Trace with no Crystal behind it, while the mourner cannot. Its Gravetide Ink drinks lamplight.

options.label: Seamless to the mourner
options.consequence: The likeness is written exactly as the living man, through the mourner's eyes; only the room (the dim lamp, the ink) hints. The horror is what the reader knows and she does not.
options.sample: Odile Marrow sat with her husband by the lamp, and he talked about the mill as he always had, the price of oats, the wheel that wanted new paddles. He rubbed his thumb along the table's edge the way he did when a sum would not come right. The lamp burned low at the rim of the circle on the floor, and its flame leaned toward the ink there and gave it nothing. She topped up the oil. The light stayed as it was.

options.label: A seam the reader catches
options.consequence: As A, plus one planted habit of the maker leaks through the likeness, findable by an attentive reader before any trained reader names it: the maker's Core as identity, made visible.
options.sample: Odile Marrow sat with her husband by the lamp, and he talked about the mill as he always had, the price of oats, the wheel that wanted new paddles. Then he said the paddles wanted feeding in by degrees, never all at once, and folded his hands on the table. Tam had never folded his hands in his life. She looked at them a long while. The lamp leaned toward the ink on the floor and gave it nothing, and she said nothing either.

options.label: A thing, plainly
options.consequence: Narration never grants the likeness the dead man's name or an inner life: it is the likeness throughout, rendered from outside as a made thing. Cold, clinical and certain.
options.sample: Odile Marrow sat across the table from the likeness by the lamp. It spoke in Tam's voice about the mill, the price of oats, the wheel that wanted new paddles. It rubbed its thumb along the table's edge. The vessel had been graded and sealed, and the seal would close on the decision it was holding whenever it found the words for it. The lamp leaned toward the ink on the floor and gave it nothing.

questions.rec_reason: The maker's Core as identity is canon, so his habit leaking through is a fair, findable tell planted before any reveal (R48-30); it keeps the mourner's grief whole while the reader starts to doubt.

settled.point: No Draft refills a reserve; alchemical treatment only speeds recovery from a Wellspring
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled twice (EC2 of the alchemy conversion restates R2-6). AL5 asks only how long using a Draft takes, never whether one refuels.

settled.point: What pays for alchemy: Drafts from stock and the site's vein; a Crystal-bearer's standing work costs a once-only share of reserve
settled.why_not_asked: EC1. AL4 builds on it: a Draft in a fight spends stock, never the thrower's reserve.

settled.point: Pure alchemists are bench-certified up to Expert, and that Tier caps their work
settled.why_not_asked: EC3. AL16 uses the cap; the Hollow-or-Expert tension (C-142) is the docket's.

settled.point: The dose is the point; the one who measures carries crucible palsy and Draft-mark
settled.why_not_asked: EC6. AL3 and AL13 use the marks as tells without re-asking them.

settled.point: Calcination and Distillation are bench operations; Sublimatio is sublimation and Sublimare distillation
settled.why_not_asked: K5 and K6 of the alchemy conversion.

settled.point: Three alchemy sources in a fixed order, The Real Alchemy written as the third
settled.why_not_asked: Method law. AL11 would add a forensic section to The Real Alchemy, not change the order.

settled.point: Residues on two clocks: four inside the Crossing's nine days, three after; a Trace is used once and reading spends the record
settled.why_not_asked: K7, DE1 and EC9. AL12 asks only how a reading reaches the page.

settled.point: A revenant is a stalled Crossing; moving the body or Stillgate Ash is the counter
settled.why_not_asked: DE6. AL17 asks only what a wound does to one.

settled.point: The impression-body: a Greater Summons, its vessel a graded Draft, a Trace-without-Crystal tell and Stillgate Ash as counter
settled.why_not_asked: DE4, DE5 and EC11. AL18 asks only how the page renders it; its two Stage floors (C-154) are the docket's.

settled.point: Mortalis Categories: Stage floors, the full cost stack, field-format entries and Bench reservation by Tier
settled.why_not_asked: EC7 to EC10.

settled.point: The Great Work's stages and currents, the Tria Prima as Crystal layers, corruptions cited by name, every corruption with a named counter
settled.why_not_asked: GW1 to GW7. AL13 asks only which signs reach the page.

settled.point: Draftcraft is written in price, vessel, seal and ledger; each author states figures as his instruments give them
settled.why_not_asked: GL4 and EC13. AL3 asks whether the habit spreads to every alchemist.

settled.point: An unentered formula is lawful to hold and unlawful to sell; the breach sits with the seller
settled.why_not_asked: EC12. AL15 uses it as a plot engine without re-asking it.

settled.point: Enhancement ceilings and item costs: an enhanced round costs its maker a share of reserve and performs no higher than his Grade; enhanced shot is standard for elites
settled.why_not_asked: Item and shot law; AL16 asks only how a thrown Draft sits beside it.

settled.point: Craft shown as process with the finished work looked at; a rite set apart as a numbered form
settled.why_not_asked: Style law of 2026-10-03. AL1 asks only whether bench work takes the rite's form.

settled.point: Prices on the page come from the approved price table, named whenever money moves
settled.why_not_asked: Approved and extended. Alchemical lots quote the Standing Index; the Alchemical Index's formulas carry no prices and none is invented here.

settled.point: Readouts: one item card, in-scene readouts at appraisal, wound and Essence spent, three a scene, body before number, clinical voice, printing instruments
settled.why_not_asked: LR17, LR8, LR9, LR12, LR4 and LR1. AL9 asks only how a Draft fits them.

settled.point: Medicine is era-appropriate by place; healing runs on real timelines and mending costs more than breaking
settled.why_not_asked: Live law. AL10 asks only where Drafts sit inside it.

settled.point: Trained POVs read the world in science terms; narration names apparatus and workings exactly
settled.why_not_asked: Settled by the writing law and VB5; AL14's chemistry rides on it.

settled.point: Money before magic and commerce on the page: the bill, the meter, branded Essence goods
settled.why_not_asked: Live law. AL2, AL6 and AL15 build on it.

settled.point: The Night Watch Society is the crown-chartered investigator of illegal workings; the Papers' Searcher is one of its officers
settled.why_not_asked: Canon institutions. AL11 and AL12 use them.

settled.point: A working's rules are shown before the fight that spends them
settled.why_not_asked: MY4. AL1 and AL4 lean on it.

settled.point: The Draft Sub-Stat profile (which Sub-Stats govern making a Draft)
settled.why_not_asked: EC4, filed for ratification through propose_rule; a design matter, not a page one.

settled.point: Open alchemy doctrine conflicts C-136 to C-154 (a Crystal at manufacture, thermometers, the decisive Crystal layer, the pure alchemist's cap, Rupture's three senses, Draft Corruption's cause, 'turn' in two senses, bench durations, the impression-body's two floors)
settled.why_not_asked: Recorded conflicts are ruled on the docket under the wotr-conflict precedence ladder (CLAUDE.md, 2026-09-25), not by questionnaire. AL2 steps round C-137 and AL18 round C-154.
